what_its_for: Finerenone is used to protect your kidneys and heart if you have chronic kidney disease (CKD) caused by type 2 diabetes. It helps reduce the risk of your kidneys getting worse, kidney failure, and serious heart problems like heart attack or hospitalization due to heart failure.
how_to_take: Take finerenone by mouth, with or without food. Swallow the tablet whole. If you have trouble swallowing the tablet whole, you may crush it and mix it with water or soft foods like applesauce, and take it right away. Do not store the crushed mixture for later use.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your kidney function (a blood test called eGFR). The usual doses are 10 mg or 20 mg once daily. Your doctor may adjust your dose after checking your potassium blood levels. Always take exactly the dose your doctor prescribed and do not change it on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember on the same day. If you do not remember until the next day, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at your regular time. Never take two doses in one day to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store finerenone tablets at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep the tablets in their original container with the lid tightly closed. Keep this medicine out of reach of children and pets. Do not store it in the bathroom or near heat or moisture.
what_to_avoid: Avoid eating large amounts of grapefruit or drinking grapefruit juice while taking this medicine, as it can increase the amount of finerenone in your blood and raise the risk of side effects. Avoid potassium supplements or salt substitutes that contain potassium unless your doctor says it is okay, because finerenone can raise potassium levels in your blood. Tell your doctor about all other medicines you take, especially certain antifungal medicines (like ketoconazole or itraconazole), certain antibiotics (like clarithromycin), HIV medicines, or St. John's Wort, as these can interact with finerenone.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or get emergency help if you have: muscle weakness, numbness or tingling, a slow or irregular heartbeat, or feel very tired or confused — these may be signs of high potassium (hyperkalemia), which can be serious. Also call your doctor if you feel dizzy or lightheaded, notice swelling in your legs or feet, have difficulty breathing, or if you think you might be pregnant. Tell your doctor before starting finerenone if you have adrenal gland problems or take certain medicines that affect potassium levels.
when_it_works: Finerenone starts working in your body shortly after you take it, but the benefits to your kidneys and heart build up over time — usually over several months. You may not feel any different right away. It is important to keep taking it every day even if you feel well, because it is working to slow down kidney damage and protect your heart in the background.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Finerenone can harm an unborn baby. If you can become pregnant, use effective birth control while taking this medicine and tell your doctor right away if you become pregnant. Do not breastfeed while taking finerenone, as it may pass into breast milk and harm your baby. Kidney or liver problems: Your doctor will monitor your kidney function and potassium levels closely and may adjust your dose. Older adults: Older patients should be watched more carefully for high potassium levels and changes in kidney function.
